notes: Our seq model assumes consecutive/contiguous ids. A git revert of a commit that added events (updates + new task creates) removes those lines from mutations.jsonl, leaving GAPS in the seq sequence. verify_seq_order only checks strictly-increasing, so gaps pass silently. Worse, a revert is effectively a mid-log deletion, which the append-only union merge does NOT model: merging a reverted branch with one that still has those events could resurrect or lose them depending on the fork point. ACTION: revalidate the entire merge algorithm (fork split, restack, watermark W=min(seq)-1, baseline keep-ours) against reverts, cherry-picks, rebases, and any history rewrite that removes or reorders events; decide whether seq must stay contiguous (and how to enforce/repair) or the algorithm must tolerate gaps.
title: Reconsider seq-contiguity assumption: git revert creates gaps that may break merge

notes: DECISION (from analysis): seq stays strictly-increasing but is NOT required to be contiguous. The merge/compaction code already tolerates gaps because every seq computation is extremum- or position-based: max(seq)+1 minting, fork = max(ancestor seq), filtering by seq vs fork, renumber-to-contiguous tail in assemble, and watermark = min(seq)-1. verify_seq_order intentionally allows gaps. A git revert that drops committed events leaves gaps, and the normal case (reverted event still present in both logs) converges in both merge directions -- covered by the revert_converges tests (merge.rs unit + e2e). SCOPE: (1) record this gap-tolerance decision durably in the Core invariants section of CLAUDE.md and in a comment near verify_seq_order / removed_seqs; (2) add characterization/edge tests: multiple gaps (revert two separate events), revert of the event at the fork boundary, revert of a Create while keeping its Updates (orphans produced via the revert path), empty-log-after-revert (revert the initial commit -> empty mutations.jsonl, min/watermark None path), and a test pinning the current revert-then-compact behavior. KNOWN LIMITATION documented (not fixed) here: revert-then-compact-past-it hides the removal below the watermark and can resurrect the event or diverge by merge direction; the fix lives in task merge-revert-compact-detector. Full prose design goes in task protocol-doc.
title: Document the seq gap-tolerance decision and cover revert/gap edges with tests

notes: removed_seqs (merge.rs) only treats an ancestor event as reverted if it sits ABOVE the branch's compaction watermark (min(seq)-1); anything below is assumed folded into the baseline. So if a branch reverts an event and LATER compacts past it, the revert goes invisible: merging against a branch that still carries the event resurrects it, and the outcome depends on merge direction (breaking the convergence guarantee). Gated by keep_events -- you must compact more than keep_events past the revert -- so it is rare but currently silent. ACTION: at merge time we have ancestor + ours + theirs, so detect the ambiguous case (an ancestor event absent from one branch BELOW that branch's watermark while still present in the other branch's shared region, seq <= fork) and warn loudly instead of silently resurrecting/diverging -- the same no-silent-failure approach as the seq-reuse warning in content_mismatches and the orphan warnings. Decide whether to only warn or also surface/fail the merge. Add an e2e test that reproduces revert-then-compact-past and asserts the warning fires. Analysis recorded in task seq-gaps-revert.
title: Detect and warn on reverted-then-compacted events at merge time

ROOT CAUSE: removed_seqs (merge.rs) only treats an ancestor event as reverted if it sits ABOVE the branch's min-seq watermark (min(seq)-1); anything below is assumed folded into the baseline by compaction. So any revert that raises a branch's min seq above the reverted seq is invisible -- TWO triggers: (a) reverting the branch's EARLIEST event(s) (no compaction needed -- see the revert_below_the_watermark_is_not_yet_detected unit test), and (b) reverting an event and LATER compacting past it. In both, merging against a branch that still carries the event resurrects it, and the outcome depends on merge direction (breaking convergence). Trigger (a) needs no compaction at all, so it is more reachable than first thought; (b) is gated by keep_events. Currently silent. ACTION: at merge time we have ancestor + ours + theirs, so detect the ambiguous case (an ancestor event absent from one branch BELOW that branch's watermark while still present in the other branch's shared region, seq <= fork) and warn loudly instead of silently resurrecting/diverging -- same no-silent-failure approach as the seq-reuse warning in content_mismatches and the orphan warnings. Decide whether to only warn or also surface/fail the merge. Add an e2e repro that asserts the warning fires. Analysis and characterization tests are in task seq-gaps-revert (merge.rs).

RESOLUTION (won't implement): a sound log-only detector is infeasible. The shape it would key on -- an ancestor event absent from a branch BELOW that branch's min-seq watermark while still present in the other branch -- is ALSO produced by ordinary compaction when two branches fold to different depths (verified against the baseline_keep_ours_merges_after_both_branches_compact test: the boundary event is folded into one branch's baseline but kept live in the other's log). Telling a real revert from a compaction fold requires that branch's BASELINE (event present there = folded/safe; absent = reverted/dangerous), and the log merge driver is handed only the mutation logs (%O %A %B), never the baseline. A baseline-aware detector (git show MERGE_HEAD:.taska/baseline.jsonl etc.) would work but couples the pure log driver to git refs and the baseline and cripples the merge unit tests. Given the bug is rare (revert below the watermark AND a concurrent branch that kept the event), we accept and document it instead. Documented in CLAUDE.md invariants, the removed_seqs comment, and the revert_below_the_watermark_is_a_known_limitation test (all in merge.rs); the full prose write-up lives in protocol-doc.

A standalone doc (docs/MERGE.md) linked from README, short but complete: why an event log vs state snapshots; performance (from benchmarks); what happens on merge/revert/conflict; resolution steps (surface vs latest/ours/theirs, ta resolve, orphan cleanup). Example-driven. Also cover the seq model: seqs are strictly-increasing but may have gaps (a git revert removes events); how a revert is reconciled by removal-union; and the compaction-vs-revert boundary (the min(seq)-1 watermark) including its ACCEPTED limitation -- a revert below the watermark can resurrect/diverge, and a log-only detector can't fix it because the merge driver isn't given the baseline (see the closed merge-revert-compact-detector task for the analysis). Resolves the README TODO about linking the detailed design of how the append log, merge, revert and conflict resolution work. Do this after seq-gaps-revert (done) and benchmarks.

IMPLEMENTED (sound, log-only). Added rewritten_shared_seqs(fork, ours, theirs) in merge.rs: it flags shared-region seqs present on exactly one branch, compared ONLY above both branches' min-seq watermarks. That window excludes anything either side folded into its baseline, so legitimate compaction (even to different depths) never trips it -- no false positives, no baseline needed (my earlier 'infeasible' analysis was wrong; this is the formulation from docs/seq-gaps-revert-analysis.md option 1). The driver now warns loudly when it fires, like the content_mismatches seq-reuse warning; it does NOT fail the merge, because the removal-union already reconciles the revert convergently -- the warning just surfaces that events one branch still had were dropped. Note: a revert FOLLOWED BY a new create reuses the freed seq, so that case surfaces via content_mismatches (content differs) rather than as pure absence; both paths warn. RESIDUAL blind spot (unchanged, documented): a revert BELOW the higher watermark (earliest events, or compacted-past) stays invisible -- pinned by revert_below_the_watermark_is_a_known_limitation. Tests: rewritten_shared_seqs_flags_a_reverted_shared_event, rewritten_shared_seqs_ignores_legitimate_compaction (the soundness case), and e2e merge_warns_when_one_branch_reverts_a_shared_event.

notes:
Two related output-presentation improvements for `list` and `show`.

LAYOUT: let BOTH `list` and `show` render either a COLUMNS table (today's `list`
view, format::render_human) or ROWS / vertical records (today's `show` view,
format::render_record). Add a layout flag to both (e.g. `--layout columns|rows`,
or `--rows`/`--columns`). The per-command default is configurable in `[display]`
(e.g. `list_layout` / `show_layout`) and defaults to ROWS for both. Note: today
list=columns and show=rows, so this makes `list` default to rows.

COLOR: beautify HUMAN output with ANSI color — ON by default for a TTY, OFF via
`--no-color`. Distinct colors for `id`, `status`, and `deps`; other column/field
names bold; the list of dep values bold. CRITICAL: color is human-output only —
never colorize `--format json`/`jsonl`, and auto-disable when stdout is not a TTY
(piping, redirect) so machine output and grep stay clean. Also respect the
NO_COLOR env var convention.

THEME-SAFETY (answer to "can we use the current palette?"): yes — use the
terminal's named ANSI 16-color palette (e.g. SGR cyan/green/yellow + bold), NOT
hardcoded 24-bit RGB. Named ANSI colors are remapped by the user's terminal theme,
so they adapt to light vs dark automatically; bold is theme-agnostic. Avoid
low-contrast shades that only look right on one background; pick from the normal/
bright named colors for id/status/deps.

Implementation notes: plumb `color: bool` + `layout` through DisplayArgs/format; a
tiny in-house ANSI helper likely beats adding a crate (the project is
dependency-cautious), though owo-colors/anstream are options. Tests: assert NO
escape codes in non-TTY output and in json/jsonl, and that `--no-color` output is
clean. Could be split into two tasks (layout, color) if it gets large.
title: list/show: columns-or-rows layout (configurable, default rows) + theme-safe color

notes:
Add a `subtask_of` (parent/child hierarchy) relationship type. For GRAPH traversal
it behaves like a blocker dependency (a parent isn't done until its children are;
effectively the child blocks the parent). BUT it expresses a tighter, human-facing
CONTAINMENT relationship, not a plain dependency.

KEY REQUIREMENT: in ALL human outputs (list, show, dep tree/list) subtasks must
look DISTINCT from blocker/dependency edges — nested/indented under the parent, a
different label/glyph/color, or a dedicated hierarchy view — so the parent/child
structure is obvious and never confused with depends_on. Likely a new config kind
beyond blocker/info (a "hierarchy"/"parent" kind) or a declared type with special
rendering.

Mostly valuable for people's mental model (grouping work under a parent); likely
low extra value for an AI agent beyond the dependency behavior it already gets.
Decide whether a parent rolls up status/progress from children (ties into
dep-traversal-features). Get the semantics right before shipping. Coordinates with
relationship-types and dep-command.
title: subtask_of (parent/child) relationship: hierarchy, rendered distinctly from deps

notes:
Graph-traversal features over the blocker DAG (and symmetric info edges), built on
relationship-types/dep-command. High value for agent planning — they answer "what
next / what's the plan / what unblocks the most":
- Impact / leverage: per task, the transitive count of tasks it (eventually)
  blocks. Surface as a `ta list` derived column and a `--sort` key ("finish this
  to unblock N").
- `ta plan <goal>` (or `dep plan`): the transitive prerequisite subgraph of a goal
  task, topologically ordered — "do exactly these, in this order".
- Critical path: `ta dep critical <goal>` — longest chain of incomplete
  prerequisites. With a numeric `estimate` task field, sum it along the path for an
  ETA + slack (CPM). No model change — just reads a field.
- blocked_by / blocking counts as derived columns; one-step lookahead ("what
  becomes ready if I close X?").
- Clusters over symmetric info types (relates_to/duplicates): connected components
  -> "related groups" / "duplicate groups".
All derive from existing edges — no new config beyond relationship-types. Mostly
graph.rs plus new dep/list surfaces.
title: Graph traversal: impact rank, ta plan, critical path, blocked-by/blocking counts

notes:
Add a `ta config validate` command to run after manually editing
.taska/config.toml. The SAME validation must also run automatically inside
`ta config set` BEFORE the change is applied (reject a bad edit rather than persist
it).

Beyond today's struct-level checks (keep_events floor), this LOADS THE WHOLE TASK
GRAPH and verifies it is consistent with the config: every relationship edge in the
log uses a declared type, blocker edges form no cycle, inverse names resolve, etc.
So removing/renaming a relationship type that tasks still use — or any config that
would make the graph invalid — is caught up front.

This is the extension point for `type-schemas`: that task plugs per-type field
schema validation into the same path. Design: a `validate_against(state)` that
takes the materialized task map; both `config validate` and `config set` call it;
keep the cheap struct-only `validate()` for the can't-lock-yourself-out path
(resolve / config get). Decide the report format (list each problem found).
title: 'ta config validate' + auto-validate in 'config set' (whole task graph vs config)

notes:
Investigate and optimize the memory/allocation overhead of per-task relationship
storage. Each TaskState now carries `depends_on: Vec<String>` plus a
`relationships: BTreeMap<String, Vec<String>>` for other typed edges. The empty
map is lazy (no heap until the first insert), so tasks with only depends_on edges
pay ~no allocation — but profile the AGGREGATE over large stores and the
with-relationships case (BTreeMap nodes + per-type Vecs + duplicated type-name
Strings). Consider flatter/cheaper representations: a single Vec<(type, target)>
(smallvec for the common small case), interned/shared type-name strings, or
unifying depends_on into one compact edge list. DO THIS AFTER `benchmarks` so
changes are measured, not guessed.
title: Optimize per-task relationship storage allocations (after benchmarks)

notes:
ALSO — string interning to numeric ids (run-local). Intern strings at load and use
numbers in the in-memory graph/maps: (1) relationship type names — enumerate the
declared types at start and use a small int id per type instead of storing the type
String in every per-task map entry; (2) task ids — generate temporary in-memory
numeric ids for tasks and store those in dep edges / the graph instead of repeating
the String id everywhere. These ids are regenerated each run and stable for the
run's duration; they NEVER touch the on-disk log/baseline (which stay string-keyed).
Cuts allocation and speeds traversal (integer keys/edges vs String). Measure with
benchmarks first.

INVERSE behavior (confirmed requirements): (1) Removal by reverse name — when
`a depends_on b`, `ta dep remove b blocks=a` must remove the SAME underlying edge
(a depends_on b). Same idea as symmetric removal: resolve the edge by
(type-or-its-inverse, endpoint) from EITHER side. (2) Bidirectional OUTPUT — every
view must show BOTH directions: `a depends_on b` and, on b, `b blocks a` (the
inverse name). For symmetric types the inverse name is the type's own name; for
one-way types (inverse empty) the reverse isn't surfaced. Implement via read-time
mirroring (like timestamp injection) keyed on the configured `inverse`.

Fold the top-level `ta ready` command into a `ta list --ready` flag, mirroring how `search` folded into `list`.

- `--ready` filters to ready tasks: not-done tasks whose every existing dependency is done. Reuse `graph::ready_tasks` (and, once blocker-typed relationships gate readiness, that same path).
- Combinable with the normal `list` criteria; `--ready` already implies not-done, so it subsumes `--open`.
- Ordering decision: `ready` returns topological order (deps before dependents) while `list` defaults to `--sort create_time`. Either keep topo order when `--ready` is set and no explicit `--sort` is given, or document that `--ready` uses the normal list sort. Pick one.
- After: remove the `ready` command; update e2e, tutorials, README, CLAUDE.md. Keep `status`'s ready count (it calls `ready_tasks` directly, independent of the CLI command).

Priority: lower than the relationships tasks — do all relationship-related work first.
title: Fold 'ta ready' into 'ta list --ready'

notes:
Polish `ta dep tree` rendering (the tree currently prints bare ids, oldest-first, all tasks, no color):

- Show only OPEN (not-done) tasks by default; `--all` includes done tasks. Design note: a done node in the middle of a chain has open descendants — decide whether to hide done nodes entirely (treating their subtree as resolved) or keep them as collapsed markers. Default proposal: hide done tasks (remaining-work view), `--all` shows everything.
- Support `--sort <field>` and `--reverse` for sibling/root ordering (reuse the `format` sort/column resolution used by `list`). Today siblings follow `depends_on` insertion order.

- Colored output for readability (color by status and/or edge type and/or depth). Must be theme-safe and honor `--no-color`/`NO_COLOR`. Reuse the color infra from `output-layout-and-color` (named palette + `--no-color`) — coordinate with / depend on that task rather than inventing a second color path.

Relationships-related; do alongside the other relationship/dep tasks.
